messages.subject: Fitting a Hierarchical Bayesian model with spatial component using R-INLA
messages.subject_clean: Fitting a Hierarchical Bayesian model with spatial component using R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have to fit couple of customized Bayesian Hierarchical Models. So I was wondering if there is any easy ways to do those in R-Inla? One of my model specification is stated below:

#################################################################################################################
Y_i ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2) # i=1, 2, ..., 517 areas
mui= X*beta+ psi_i +epsilon_i  # beta be the fixed covariate effect, psi_i is the spatial random effect and epsilon_i is non-spatial residual

#priors:
epsilon_i ~(iid) N(0, 1/sigma_epsilon_i)
psi_i ~ MVN (nu, tau*Sigma) #tau>0 is the precision parameter that controls the overall variability of psi_i
Sigma_ij=exp[-(vd_ij)^k] #  k (0<k<2, usually taken as k=2) provides the extent of spatial smoothing and d_ij denotes the distances between centroids of areas i and j

#Hyperpriors: the hyperpriors for
sigma_i^2 ~ 2* S_i^2/Chisq(2) # Si^2 be the sample variances of Y_i
sigma_epsilon_i~ Gamma(0.5,0.0005)
tau ~ Ga,mma(0.001,0.001)
k~Unif(0.05,1.95)
v~Unif(0.05,20)
############################################################################################################################

Can anyone suggest me the formula or command I need to use for fitting this type of models in R-INLA?

Thanks and regards,
Farzana.

People don't usually ask for models like this since the mean-model mu_i and the variance model sigma_i are too confounded to be identifiable.

If you have a massive amount of data (in the right sense, whatever that is in this case) you may try to ad-hoc estimate sigma_i, and then use INLA with those estimates as known fixed values.

Best,

messages.subject: Predicting mean values on grid/holding out data to determine model fit
messages.subject_clean: Predicting mean values on grid/holding out data to determine model fit
messages.body_plain:
I'm working on an INLA analysis in which I'm trying to determine which environmental variables best predict timing of breeding (day of year) in a falcon species. I found that my best model included a fixed effect of start-of-spring index (day of year that leaf out occurs) and a spatial random effect. I'm interested in eventually using the model to predict laydates across my study area. I've tried to follow a few tutorials to predict the posterior mean and SD onto a map, but I'm having some trouble getting my model to do that. I've included my code and data here that gets me right up to that point.

Right now I'm trying to follow this example, but I'm not sure how to alter my code to do it: https://www.stat.washington.edu/peter/591/INLA.html

I was also wondering about determining model fit by holding out a subset of the data. Would it be reasonable to make predictions with the model (map estimated laydate across my study area) and use something like RMSE to see how well the model values match the actual withheld laydates?

My predictor variable (start-of-spring index) is available as a raster layer across my study area. Could I use that for prediction instead of using inla.mesh.projector?

Thanks,

Jay

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
You’d need to to project/evaluate the field on the mesh at some point, but there are several options for how/when/where to do that. I see you’re already using inlabru for some plotting; you might consider using it for the estimation as well, as it should make the posterior prediction a lot easier and flexible; you may need to convert the raster to SpatialPixelsDataFrame, but see the tutorial examples on inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> for how to do that and setup such a model and do prediction.
(In the development version of inlabru one can actually use predict() on regular inla() output, but the raster/SpatialPixels handling I think requires setting up the model in inlabru format)

Finn

messages.subject: Berkson measurement error model with inla.stack and multiple effects blocks
messages.subject_clean: Berkson measurement error model with inla.stack and multiple effects blocks
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to run a model that includes an SPDE model, fixed effects, and a (heteroscedastic) Berkson error model. I am using separate effects blocks in inla.stack for the SPDE model and the rest [i.e. stack = inla.stack( ... A=list(A.est, 1) ... ) ].

The NAs in stack$effects$data$w seem to cause an error for the meb model, as the values are not unique.

A minimal example (using a fixed effect for z, in place of the SPDE model):

#######################################################################
n <- 10
w <- 20 + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
s <- c(rep(2, n/2), rep(3, n/2))
z <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
y <- 10 + z + 3*(w + rnorm(n, 0, 1)) + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

stack <- inla.stack(data    = list(y = y),
                    A       = list(1, 1),
                    effects = list(list(z = z, intercept = 1),
                                   list(w = w, s = s)),
                    tag     = "t")

result <- inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s, values = w),
               control.predictor = list(A       = inla.stack.A(stack),
                                        link    = 1,
                                        compute = TRUE),
               data = inla.stack.data(stack))
#######################################################################

Gives the error:

> Error in inla(y ~ -1 + intercept + z + f(w, model = "meb", scale = s,  :
>   The 'values' given in f(w,..., values=...) are not unique:
>     length(values)=20 but length(unique(values))=11

Is there any workaround for this? Or should I be specifying the model in some other way?

Regards,
Neil

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I think you're getting bitten by the scoping rules for the formula:
f(w, ..., values=w) will use the same w vector in both places, but
what you need is for the first one to be what the stack provides, and
the values one to be your original w-vector. Use different names for
them, e.g.
  list(ww = w, s = s)
in the stack and
  f(ww, ..., values=w)
in the formula.

Finn

messages.subject: Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.subject_clean: Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am slightly confused about the link parameter in `inla` for `control.family` and `control.predictor`. From reading the FAQ, I understand that (feel free to correct if anything is inaccurate):

- `control.family(control.link = "<name of link function")`: determines the link function between the predictor `eta` and the mean `mu`, such as `identity`, `logit`, `log-link`, `log`, etc. We can see all the available links with `lapply(inla.models()$likelihood, function(x) x$link)`

- `control.predictor(link = 1)`: determines the index of the family which should use for computing the posterior of the distribution

My questions are:

1) If we are estimating a model with a single likelihood family (say, "gaussian"), do we still need to supply the link index to `control.predictor` or the default is to have `link = 1`? When do we need to supply an argument when we have an estimation with a single family?

2) The documentation says that if an element of the response vector is not null then the corresponding entry in `link` is ignored. Is this because it knows which family an observation which is not null belongs to? But if the later is true, why would it not know the corresponding family for those values which are null given that they are defined in the same dataset (say `Y`)?

3) We can always use `inla.marginal.transform` or any other function that operates on the posterior to estimate posterior predictions of the observations. On the other hand, we cannot easily add custom link functions to `control.family`, it has to be one of the listed options. Is that correct?

4) Is there anywhere in the docs an explanation about how to implement custom link functions for linking `eta` to the likelihood function?

Thanks in advance for your help.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.body_plain:
For 1) and 2), link is only needed for NA “observations”, but there is no harm in specifying it for actual observations. You are correct that for a single likelihood model, it would be reasonable for inla to infer that link=1 is intended for all elements, but there are use cases where this isn’t a reasonable assumption (when predicting parts of the linear predictor, for which the link function doesn’t make sense, and might result in NaN etc). For this and other historical reasons, the user must explicitly specify it.

3) yes, link functions need to be explicitly implemented. Marginal.transform isn’t as accurate as doing it within the inla call.

4) I’m not sure...

Finn

Thanks again for the quick reply!

Now I understand the `link` argument better. There is one thing which remains unclear after re-reading your answer and the FAQ.

When the `link` argument is not passed to `control.predictor`, INLA will use the identity link for the `NA` observations. In such cases, INLA even display a warning message.

However, how can INLA produce posterior for the fitted values using the identity link function in cases for which the likelihood is not defined? Let me give a concrete example to be clearer.

In the FAQ, the Tokyo dataset is used to illustrate prediction with INLA <http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-How-can-I-do-predictions-using-INLA->. The aim is to model the variable `y` using a binomial likelihood. The binomial likelihood is parameterised by a probability p which must be between 0 and 1. So if we use the identity link function for estimating the posterior of fitted values (that is, p(y | theta) ), it is not clear to me what is being estimated since the likelihood at values outside of the interval [0, 1] is not defined, or to be more precise it is 0.

Thus, what kind of posterior is being estimated by INLA in this case, since p(y | theta) > 0 for values outside of the range of the Binomial distribution which is our assumption for p(y | theta). messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Difference between Link Parameter in control.family and control.predictor
messages.body_plain:
On 3 May 2018 at 19:57, <guilherm...@flowminder.org> wrote:

> Ok, so for NA observations what is the assumed likelihood function, p(y_i | theta)? Is that the same as for the linear predictor p(eta_i | theta)?

There are no likelihood models at all associated with NA "observations".  They are only used to indicate that there is a linear predictor eta_i that
_would_have_ been associated with an observation if it hadn't been NA.

> So for estimation purposes we would have something like this:
>
> > p(y | theta) = p(y_1 | theta) x ... x p(y_i | theta) x p(y_i+1 | theta) x ... x p(y_n | theta)
>
> > p(y | theta) = Bin(g(eta_1) | theta) x ... x Bin(g(eta_i) | theta) x p(eta_i | theta) x ... x p(eta_n | theta)

Rather, for each "i" for which y_i is not NA,
  p(y_i | eta_i, theta) ~ Bin(Ntrials_i, g^{-1}(eta_i)), conditionally independent across all "i", given eta and theta.

For y_i that is NA  there is no likelihood, and hence no link function, unless the user says that these missing values
_are_ indeed associated with something for which applying the same link function as for the non-NA y_i:s is meaningful.

(At least I think that's the common way of defining the direction of the link function; g(location parameter for y) = linear predictor
It fits the "logit link" language...)

Finn

Hello,

I'm trying to implement LatticeKrig in INLA as an rgeneric model, but I'm running into an issue where INLA seems to run forever. If there were an error message, it would probably be easier to fix, but since there isn't I'm not sure what's going wrong. The last message that INLA gives before freezing up is:

"Called from: eval(expr, p)"

and comes after loading the required packages and libraries into the rgeneric model. I checked the dimension of the A and Q matrices, and their largest dimension is only 1228 in the full stack. Also, there are only 2 hyperparameters as currently implemented. Interestingly, the INLA process doesn't appear to be using my computer's CPU, but is using at most 200 megabytes of memory. Also, the amount of memory used decreases with the runtime. I've attached part of the code leading up to the INLA call, along with the output after the call to INLA. Any idea what could be going wrong? Any help would be much appreciated.

Thanks!

-Johnny

P.S. This is only part of the code, but I can always send more if necessary.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can we have INLA switch to a local search?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can we have INLA switch to a local search?
messages.body_plain:
hi

sorry for joining late.

this option, 'stupid search', was added to rescue difficult cases.
the alg goes like this:

- run the optimizer to get the estimated mode
- estimate the hessian at this mode
- if the '-hessian' is pos def, return. if its NOT pos def, we have not
a mode, THEN switch to the stupid search mode:

	S:
	- look at all the func-evals used to estimate the hessian.
	- move to the mode within those
	- re-estimate the hessian at this new point.
	- if `-hessian', positive definite, return, else, go back to S.

as you see, this should not happen, and if it does, it will go into a
sloooow loop, but it will not stop because of 'mode not found'.

so the issue is really to prevent the alg going into 'stupid search
mode'. when it goes into that mode, it usually means that the log-
posterior is very flat. more informative priors will do wonders, but it
can also be that a to flexible model is used.

hope this helps
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

See inline.

On 30 April 2018 at 20:42, Carrie Perkins <cp...@terpmail.umd.edu> wrote:

> Thank you both so much! I think I finally got it to work using a mixture of both of your code, plus guidance from this post: https://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/187798/create-polygons-of-the-extents-of-a-given-raster-in-r
>

> I do have a few additional questions: each pixel in my original raster was 100m by 100m and I have covariate data for each pixel that I want to use in an R inla bayesian spatial regression model. Does that mean that there should be a triangle for each pixel? If yes, should I change the max edge to 100?

No. The triangles are only for representing the spatial random effect. You can still observe pixels. Just pretend they are locations and at each location you have covariate values.

>
> Also, what determines the amount of land the mesh stretches over in the Haakon Bakka model? Is the short correlation range dictated by the cutoff being 1/5 of the max edge?

The cutoff is related to the approximation of the coastline. How far you stretch the mesh over land is the same as if you didi a stationary model.  What you have seems reasonable.

>
> Is this mesh only used to help the model decide where to predict the results spatially, or does the extent of the mesh need to match the data points perfectly?

It is only used for the spatial random effect. You can only predict or fit data in the "inner" part of the mesh. Where exactly you have datapoints (or prediction points) is mostly irrelevant (as long as it is not outside the inner mesh).

Haakon

Hi,

I cannot guess the error based on the error output, unfortunately. Can you try out
- num.threads=1
- having a different prediction and estimation length
- remove the intercept from the stack and the formula
- Making sure you have enough memory in your computer

If you try one of them at a time, that could tell us why it crashes.

By the way, what is your mesh$n and k?

Best,
Haakon

For having 'besag' prior for the regression coefficients you do need to create one areal index for each one. Them use it in the formula as

  f(idx1, x1, model='besag', ...) + f(idx2, x2, model='besag', ...) + ...

Elias

On 08/05/2018 04:48, studywo...@gmail.com wrote:

> Hello,
> Thank you so much for your prompt reply.
> If I include 5 variables, My model is y = beta1*x1 + beta2*x2 + beta3*x3 + beta4*x4.
> And I want to add the CAR prior on beta1, beta2, beta3 and beta4, the 4 effects are not independent. And the adjacent matrix is a 4*4 dimension. if my adjacent matrix is as follows:
>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
> [1,]    1    1    1    0
> [2,]    1    1    0    0
> [3,]    1    0    1    1
> [4,]    0    0    1    1
>
> Then the priors is like: beta1 ~ N((beta2+beta3)/2, q^2), beta2 ~  N(beta1, q^2), beta3 ~  N((beta1+beta4)/2, q^2), beta4 ~  N(beta3, q^2), q^2 ~ InvGama(1,1)
>
> And as what I have seen in other's code,  f(idx, z, model=”besag”, graph=…, scale.model=TRUE, constr=FALSE) refers to the model as follows:
> y = beta1*x1, and the CAR model is add on the several realization values of the beta1. And this is different from my model.
>
> Could you please give me a brief description of the solution? Any help would be much appreciated.
>
> Best Regards.

messages.body_plain:
Only if I use two effects blocks in the stack as follows

effects = list(list(z = z, intercept = 1), list(w = w, s = s))

then

f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s, values=w)

gives the error "The 'values' given in f(w,..., values=...) are not unique"
and
f(w, model  = "meb", scale = s)

gives the error "Error: length(random.spec$values) == ns is not TRUE"

If I use one effects block in the stack

effects = list(list(z=z, intercept=1, w=w, s=s))

then both models work, but give different results.

messages.body_plain:
As far as I can tell, the only correct combination in the thread so
far is a slight modification of the following one, where w and s are
_not_ part of the stack, since they describe the model itself, and
_not_ information for each observation:

"using list(ww = w, ss = s) in the stack and  f(ww, ..., scale=s,
values=w) in the formula, there is no error."

Just use
  list(ww=w_for_each_observation)
in the stack, and
  f(ww, scale=s, values=w)
where (w[k], s[k]) are pairs of w-values and their corresponding s-values.
These should _not_ be constructed with inla.stack.

At least that's what I take from the inla.doc("meb") text, for how to
construct a heteroscedastic model (the scale values seem to go into
the D matrix there, even though that's not explicitly spelled out).

Finn

Hi,

The length of the index vector has to be the same size of the data, unless you work with projections such the case we have with SPDE models. Specifically, you have to specify to which one of the elements in the graph each observation belongs to. Example: idx1 = rep(1:4, each=25) is the case where the first 25 observations belongs to the first node, the observations from 26 to 50 to the second one, and so on.

Elias

messages.body_plain:
I agree with Elias, that while your code might now _run_, it doesn't
actually estimate the model you wanted to estimate.

Looking through the thread, I believe what you're looking for are
correlated spatially varying covariate effects.
For simplicity, assuming one observation for each spatial graph node,
and only 3 covariates:

y_i = x_{1i} beta_{1j} + x_{2i} beta_{2j} + x_{3i} beta_{3j} + epsilon_i

where the spatial beta-fields have a kronecker product precision structure,

Q_beta = Q_dependence %x% Q_besag
or
Q_beta = Q_besag %x% Q_dependence

where Q_dependence is related to what you in an earlier email called
"the adjacency matrix" for the beta:s.
(I'm not sure how to turn your "adjacency matrix" into a precision;
need more details of precisely what model you want!)

The second form of the kronecker type model can be implemented using
something like this:

y ~ f(beta_index, covariate_value, model="generic0", Cmatrix=Q_dependence,
        group = spatial_index, control.group=list(model="besag", graph
= ..., ...))

where beta_index is
  beta_index = rep(1:3, each=spatial_size)
and covariate_value is the vector of covariate values across the
spatial graph, with first all the x_1-values, then the x_2-values,
etc.

PS. This confusion is precisely why Haakon's suggestion in the
beginning of the thread is so important:
  When in doubt, or when it's difficult to explain, spell out all the
mathematical details of your model!

Finn

> >

Does that mean that there should be a triangle for each pixel? If yes, should I change the max edge to 100?
>
> No. The triangles are only for representing the spatial random effect. You can still observe pixels. Just pretend they are locations and at each location you have covariate values.
>
>
> >
> > Also, what determines the amount of land the mesh stretches over in the Haakon Bakka model? Is the short correlation range dictated by the cutoff being 1/5 of the max edge?
>
> The cutoff is related to the approximation of the coastline. How far you stretch the mesh over land is the same as if you didi a stationary model.  What you have seems reasonable.
>
> >
> > Is this mesh only used to help the model decide where to predict the results spatially, or does the extent of the mesh need to match the data points perfectly?
>
>
> It is only used for the spatial random effect. You can only predict or fit data in the "inner" part of the mesh. Where exactly you have datapoints (or prediction points) is mostly irrelevant (as long as it is not outside the inner mesh).
>

>
> Haakon

I am running an model in inlabru, using the function lgcp with a SPDE field. This  <https://www.dropbox.com/s/ytuevt7dgvn4qba/Rplot.jpeg?dl=1>is what my data looks like. These animals never fly over land, which is why I have removed the outer boundary to the east and inside the islands.The mesh is generated with this code:

boundary_in <- inla.sp2segment(b_in)
boundary_out <- inla.sp2segment(b_out)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = list(boundary_in, boundary_out), # these are SpatialPolygons (attached)
                     max.edge = c(70, 200),                      # max edge in the inner boundary is approx. the expected range/5
                       cutoff = 10)                                       # any value larger than this and the boundaries of the islands start to lose too much its shape

And the model is run with this:

# specify the 2d matérn field for the random effect
matern2d <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                                prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01),  #specified that sd is unlikely to be larger than 0.1
                                prior.range = c(20, 0.1))    # we don't want our model picking up spatial structures at ranges smaller than 20 km.

# specify the components
cmp0 <- coordinates ~ mySPDE(map = coordinates, model = matern2d) +
                      Intercept

# fit the model
fit0 <- lgcp(components = cmp0,
             data = ds.df2,     # spatial points dataframe (attached)
             samplers = bound)  # same polygon as the inner boundary (also attached)

Everything seems to run according to plan but when I try to predict the intensity with

lmbd0 <- predict(fit0, pixels(mesh, mask = T), ~exp(Intercept + mySPDE))

and try to plot it using the ggplot functions

ggplot() + gg(lmbd0["median"]) + coord_equal()

I get the error message

Error in if ((w[1] * sm + w[2] * cm + w[3] * dm + w[4]) < best$score) break : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Trying to plot it outside ggplot with

plot(lmbd0["median])
plot(bound, border = "white", add = T)

Hi,

I believe in your suspicion that it runs into problems due to the
geometry being tricky with so many points close to the boundary, but
I'll keep investigating why it fails so spectacularly.
Also, could you send me the example code for the 2km expanded buffer
as well? 2km however is a tiny buffer, since cutoff is 10 km.  A 20km
buffer would be more reasonable (but see below about other model
options).

Predicting on the log-scale shows the problem more clearly:

  ggplot() + gg(lmbd1["median"]) + coord_equal()
As you noted, there's a single hotspot near the coast where the model
breaks down. In the past, such hotspots were the cause of an invalid
numerical integration scheme in the lgcp likelihood approximation, but
the current method shouldn't behave like this.
Predicting log(abs(...)), just to see if there is any pattern hiding
underneath, does show a pattern that connects reasonably well to the
actual point pattern, so it seems it's just the one hotspot that cases
some numerical issue.

Since the current CRAN version, we have fixed a few minor bugs,
available in the development version; see
https://github.com/fbachl/inlabru/tree/devel for installation
instructions,
but since I was running the development version, this clearly did not
help in this case.

much better with this kind of situation; several recent threads
discuss those.
As far as I'm aware of, noone has used them in combination with
inlabru yet, but I'm keen to get those working, so if you try them and
run into problems, please let me know!
In principle, they should work seamlessly with inlabru::lgcp(), but
the inner workings of the inlabru&inla code may complain a bit...

me verify that your coordinate system makes sense!)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think I've identified the issue:
Since the mesh building simplifies the boundary, there is a mismatch
between the actual mesh boundary and the specified "samplers" domain,
which is the original, high-resolution boundary shape.
In principle, this shouldn't be an issue as long as the mismatch is
small, but it seems it results in some badly scaled integration
weights near the boundary; e.g., a too small integration weight in the
vicinity of an observed point should result in precisely the behaviour
we see, where the intensity is dragged towards infinity; it simply
isn't penalised in the approximate likelihood like it would be in the
true likelihood.

There are some related issues for calculating the integration weights
that interacts with this, making it difficult to debug, so a proper
solution may need to wait until I have more time to clean up the code
and make it more robust to edge cases like this (our original inlabru
package developer has moved on to work in a bank...).

The "barrier" models can have meshes that extend inland, which should
eliminate the problem even with the current inlabru integration code,
so I would suggest trying that, in particular since it removes the
edge effects that may also confuse your model, as it has an isolated
small "lake" in the southeast corner!

I'd still be interested in seeing the case with an extended domain you
mentioned, so I have more test cases to use for debugging.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
On 9 May 2018 at 00:52, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The "barrier" models can have meshes that extend inland, which should
> eliminate the problem even with the current inlabru integration code,
> so I would suggest trying that, in particular since it removes the
> edge effects that may also confuse your model, as it has an isolated
> small "lake" in the southeast corner!

Small caveat: those models should have _less_ issues of this type, but
currently, any model where the sampling domain doesn't align with the
mesh edges is liable to have this problem.
Alternative workaround is therefore to _first_ simplify the boundary
_before_ constructing the mesh, instead of letting the mesh builder do
it; that way, you have more control over the simplification, and can
supply the simplified boundary as the sampler parameter, which should
solve the problem.
inla.simplify.curve() may, or may not, be helpful for this (it doesn't
do exactly what we want in this case; it doesn't eliminate close
points)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

Thanks for all the suggestions, it seems I have a lot to do now!

The code I used to make the 2km buffer around the boundaries (which gives the same result) is:

b_in_2buff <- rgeos::gBuffer(b_in, width = 2)
b_out_2buff <- rgeos::gBuffer(b_out, width = 2)
boundary_in <- inla.sp2segment(b_in_2buff)
boundary_out <- inla.sp2segment(b_out_2buff)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = list(boundary_in, boundary_out), max.edge = c(70, 200), cutoff = 10)

I tried running it again with a buffer of 20 as you suggested, but I lose the islands completely (see attached image) and inla crashes (see other attached image) giving errors related to NAs and Infs as well:

GMRFLib version 3.0-0-snapshot, has recived error no [12]
Reason : The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message : Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
Function : GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern
File : approx-inference.c Line : 2890
RCSId : file: approx-inference.c hgid: f83f00640846 date: Tue May 08 10:16:23 2018 +0300

(All this is run with the developement version of inlabru now, and R version 3.5.0)

I suspect this might be because the boundary sort of "bends on itself" with this buffer, causing weird geometries.

I'll start trying to apply your suggestions and keep you posted of developments.

Thank you again!

Virginia Morera
PhD Student
Department of Animal Biology
University of Barcelona

While the difference in result is larger than I'd like, that test
model isn't really identifiable, which amplifies the small numerical
differences resulting from the order.
Looking at the full summary output below reveals that the result
difference for the posterior mean is around 4% of the posterior
standard deviation for the intercept, and 0.2% for z.
The relative differences for the hyperparameters is also on the order
of less than 4%.

I've also attached an experiment where I ran inla.rerun() repeatedly,
to see if it would be able to get closer to the same estimate by
continuing the optimisation.
(It gives a warning about the "meb" model that I don't see even in a
fresh R session; it's too long for the page width, but I assume it
says something about the model being experimental...).
It's clear that this model is numerically unstable due to
non-identifiability between the precision parameters.
For comparison I included a model using the same input but changed
into Poisson counts, which removes one precision parameter, and the
results comparable between the two data orderings,
with less than 0.1% relative difference for the fixed effect estimates.

messages.body_plain:
I have been trying Haakon's code for the Barrier model (script and data attached) and everything seems to run smoothly until I get to actually construct the model, using the new mesh I've created and the barrier.triangles object. When running

barrier.model = inla.barrier.pcmatern(mesh2, barrier.triangles = barrier.triangles,
                                      prior.range = c(6, 0.5),
                                      prior.sigma = c(3, 0.01))

I get the error message

Error in solve.default(t(Ts) %*% Ts) :
system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 2.89737e-21

I am pretty sure it has to do with the polygon used for my mesh having self intersections (see code attached) but I don't know how to fix that. Some posts suggest running gBuffer with width = 0, but this just gets me the outer polygon, and I lose all the islands and shapes inside.

Virginia Morera
PhD Student
Department of Animal Biology
University of Barcelona

messages.body_plain:
As an aside: With the newest version of INLA, you can run (assuming you constructed the mesh from a polygon poly.water):

water.tri = inla.over_sp_mesh(poly.water, y = mesh, type = "centroid", ignore.CRS = T)
poly.water2 = inla.barrier.polygon(mesh, barrier.triangles = barrier.tri)

The polygon you are actually using, when you are modeling the data is poly.water2. You may want to use this for plotting and determining in-out points, rather than using your original polygon. I do.

If you do the mesh for a stationary model or a barrier model, the problems you have encountered probably will not lead to any serious issues, but you may want to resolve them anyway.

Additional tips can be found at
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic104.html
and
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic127.html

Best,
Haakon

Hi Virginia,

I actually did not get your error when I ran the code. I was also able to plot the poly.barrier.

I think it is the self-intersection that is the problem (also causing the next error). Could you try some of the tricks at https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic127.html ?
Here, we use gBuffer and gIntersection and gSimplify. Maybe if you have a more complex polygon you can make sure that one is more well-defined before you make the mesh?

PS: If you plot plot(mesh2), you see that it looks quite bad. Could you try to get a mesh that looks a bit nicer (as plot(mesh) does)?

Best,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
gSimplify uses a version of the same algorithm as inla.siplify.curve that I mentioned previously, and hence is liable to the same issue: it tries to preserve non-linear/curved features while removing points that fall on straight lines, but what we would like is a method that _smooths_ the curve. I’m not aware of a good function for that.

Finn

messages.subject: Interpreting INLAs WAIC scores
messages.subject_clean: Interpreting INLAs WAIC scores
messages.body_plain:
I'm having some trouble interpreting some spatial INLA models.

Essentially, I can fit a model fine, and it looks basically plausible, but when comparing between nested models using the WAIC score, I get counter-intuitive results I don't understand. Normally, I expect that a covariate that has a strong relationship with my variable of interest should have CIs that do not overlap zero, and that when comparing between models with and without that covariate I would expect WAIC to be lower in models that include the variable. But I am consistently getting the opposite pattern in real data sets. I suspect it is something o do with correlations between variables, but I can't generate a simple dataset that replicates it based on that assumption, so it might be something to do with my data or another part of my model (though I've tweaked priors and that isn't helping). The real data that exhibit the problem are attached, and code to run it (runs in a minute or two) is below. In this example the model predicts insect richness from three covariates, two of which are quite strongly cross correlated. I would expect a successful model to identify only one of the two correlated variables as important - and sure enough the model identifies taxon_alpha as a clearly strong predictor, with phylo_alpha not adding meaningful additional information. But a model that drops taxon_alpha has a much higher WAIC that a model that drops phylo_alpha (and than the full model), suggesting the opposite is true. I can't really reconcile these two results, as usually the work fine.

library(spdep)
library(sp)
library(INLA)
library(gstat)
div.df <- source("DumpData.txt")[[1]]

neighs <- dnearneigh(as.matrix(div.df[,c("x", "y")]), longlat = TRUE, d1 = 0, d2 = 15)  #identified neighbours within 15km (i.e. queen's case adjacency)
nb2INLA( "adj.txt", neighs)

rich.analysis <- inla(c(scale(log(ins_rich))) ~ taxon_alpha.s  + phylo_alpha.s +
                        functional_alpha.s
                      + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                          hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                      #+ f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                      #    hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",
                      #                             param = c(0.1, 0.5), initial = 0.1))),
                      family = "gaussian",
                      control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                      data = div.df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
rich.analysis.noTA <- inla(c(scale(log(ins_rich))) ~ functional_alpha.s  + phylo_alpha.s
                           + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                               hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                           # + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                           #     hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",
                           #                             param = c(0.1, 0.5), initial = 0.1))),
                           family = "gaussian",
                           control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                           data = div.df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
rich.analysis.noPA <- inla(c(scale(log(ins_rich))) ~ functional_alpha.s  + taxon_alpha.s
                           + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                               hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                           # + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                           #     hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",
                           #                              param = c(0.1, 0.5), initial = 0.1))),
                           family = "gaussian",
                           control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                           data = div.df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
rich.analysis.noFA <- inla(c(scale(log(ins_rich))) ~ phylo_alpha.s  + taxon_alpha.s
                           + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                               hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                           # + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
                           #     hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "loggamma",
                           #                              param = c(0.1, 0.5), initial = 0.1))),
                           family = "gaussian",
                           control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                           data = div.df, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
summary(rich.analysis)
## taxon_alpha has the largest effect, phylo is close to zero (but strongly correlated). Functional has an independent effec

#summary(rich.analysis.noTA)
#summary(rich.analysis.noPA)
#summary(rich.analysis.noFA)
rich.analysis$waic$waic   ## Should be intermediate - need only one of phylo or taxon
rich.analysis.noTA$waic$waic    ## Should be highest - taxon is the largest effect in full model
rich.analysis.noPA$waic$waic    ## Should be lowest - all information in phylo is also recorded in taxon
rich.analysis.noFA$waic$waic    ## should be high - functional has some additional information

Thinking this may just be driven by correlation, I generated some dummy datasets that I expected would show the same effect (see below), but in these simple examples INLA works exactly as expected - whichever of the correlated variables have the largest parameter estimates in the full model are also characterised by models with low WAIC - when this variable is removed from a model the WAIC increases. This is the expected behaviour (I think) and suggests there's something odd with my real data - but I have several examples from totally different datasets where the behaviour shown above is general, so it's nothing too weird about the data...

Any solutions / hints welcome!
Thanks in advance,
Colin

### Dummy data:
set.seed(12)
library(spdep)
library(gstat)
x1 <- runif(100)
x2 <- runif(100)
x3 <- x1 + runif(100)/3
xy <- expand.grid(x = 1:10, y =1:10)
g.dummy <- gstat(formula=z~1, locations=~x+y, dummy=T, beta=1,
                 model=vgm(psill=0.025,model="Exp",range=3), nmax=20)
yy <- predict(g.dummy, newdata=xy, nsim=1)

y  <- x1  + rnorm(100)/2 + yy[,3]
y1  <- x1  + x3 + rnorm(100)/2 + yy[,3]
ID <- 1:100
neighs <-  dnearneigh(as.matrix(xy),  d1 = 0, d2 = 1.5)  #identified neighbours within 1.75km (i.e. queen's case adjacency)
nb2INLA( "dummy.txt", neighs)

dummy.data <- data.frame( y = y, y1 = y1, x1 = c(scale(x1)), x2 = c(scale(x2)),
                          x3 = c(scale(x3)), ID = ID)

# Dataset where y depends on x1 alone, but x3 is correlates with x1.
test.full <- inla(y ~ x1 + x2 +x3 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",
                                      hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                  family = "gaussian",
                  #                      lincomb = all.lincombs,
                  control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                  data = dummy.data, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
summary(test.full)

test.no.x1 <- inla(y ~  x2 +x3 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",
                                   hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                   family = "gaussian",
                   #                      lincomb = all.lincombs,
                   control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                   data = dummy.data, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
test.no.x2 <- inla(y ~  x1 + x3 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",
                                    hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                   family = "gaussian",
                   #                      lincomb = all.lincombs,
                   control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                   data = dummy.data, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
test.no.x3 <- inla(y ~  x1 + x2 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",
                                    hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.5)))),
                   family = "gaussian",
                   #                      lincomb = all.lincombs,
                   control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                   data = dummy.data, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
summary(test.full)
test.full$waic$waic  ## Should be intermediate
test.no.x1$waic$waic ## Should be highest - x1 is a predictor
test.no.x2$waic$waic ## Should be low - x2 is not a predictor
test.no.x3$waic$waic ## Should be low - x3 is not a predictor, but is correlated with x1

# dataset where y1 is dependent on both x1 and x3, but the two are pretty well confounded (r >0.9)
test.full <- inla(y1 ~ x1 + x2 +x3 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",

summary(test.full)

                   #                      lincomb = all.lincombs,
                   control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                   data = dummy.data, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))
test.no.x2 <- inla(y1 ~  x1 + x3 + f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "dummy.txt",

                   family = "gaussian",

Dear Colin,

I had a quick look at the data. Here are a few things to consider
- the relation between taxon and phylo is strong and non-linear (log linear?)
- the distribution of taxon is much more clumped than that of phylo
- as a result the phylo-functional combination covers a larger part of
the design space than the taxon-functional combination

So IMHO it is not surprising that the model selects phylo + functional
over taxon + functional

  geom_point()
ggplot(div.df, aes(x = phylo_alpha.s, y = functional_alpha.s)) +
  geom_point()

> I'm having some trouble interpreting some spatial INLA models.
>
> Essentially, I can fit a model fine, and it looks basically plausible, but
> when comparing between nested models using the WAIC score, I get
> counter-intuitive results I don't understand. Normally, I expect that a
> covariate that has a strong relationship with my variable of interest should
> have CIs that do not overlap zero, and that when comparing between models
> with and without that covariate I would expect WAIC to be lower in models
> that include the variable. But I am consistently getting the opposite
> pattern in real data sets. I suspect it is something o do with correlations
> between variables, but I can't generate a simple dataset that replicates it
> based on that assumption, so it might be something to do with my data or
> another part of my model (though I've tweaked priors and that isn't
> helping). The real data that exhibit the problem are attached, and code to
> run it (runs in a minute or two) is below. In this example the model
> predicts insect richness from three covariates, two of which are quite
> strongly cross correlated. I would expect a successful model to identify
> only one of the two correlated variables as important - and sure enough the

messages.body_plain:
Hi, that’s indeed a spectacular failure message, which isn’t only due to inlabru, but likely also issues with R 3.5.0...  but I do see some things that inlabru will definitely need: for regular spde models, it fins the mesh in the spde object, but since the barrier model is a different kind of model object that doesn’t work. You have to supply it manually to lgcp(), I believe as domain=mesh.

Can you send me the updated code so I can check on R 3.4.2?

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thanks!

the lgcp parameter should be
  domain = list(coordinates = mesh2)
instead of
  domain = mesh2

With that correction, it runs with no errors on R 3.4.2; the missing
"methods" etc warning I belive is entirely unrelated, and is issue
with either 3.5.0 or how you run the code; the command line Rscript
method used to have this problem, where it didn't load the core R
packages, to which methods and the other listed packages in your
warning message belong.  I thought they'd fixed that problem though.
How did you run the code when that warning came up? Can you run
something much more simple and see if you get the same warning (i.e.
something that doesn't involve INLA or inlabru at all).

Haakon, how should one interpret the Theta1 and Theta2 parameters for
the barrier model output? Since it's not stored as an inla.spde
object, inla.spde.result won't work, and for regular pcmatern models
inla converts the output to range and sigma.

The summary output indicates that it managed to make an estimation,
but there are clearly issues with it.
I wonder if the covering square that shows up in new_sp is causing
problems by confusing the samplers setup, see attached figure of
new_sp and the estimated myBARRIER model component.

The inlabru predict() function doesn't manage to do a spatial
prediction (just comes out as constant), so I think there is still
some code in inlabru that only does the right thing for ordinary spde
model objects; the main issue tends to be how and where it needs to
know about the mesh, which isn't present in the barrier.model object
(at least not where inlabru would expect it to be).

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Thierry,

Thanks for your thoughts on this. I can see the basic idea, but I can't quite work out why this seems so general across three entirely different datasets, and would be happier if I could simulate the problem reliably, so I know when it might be occurring. Is is the non-linearity of the cross correlation that matters (seems unlikely - univariate plots support a strong and not terribly odd linear taxon_alpha and ins_rich correlation, and one of the datasets I have been using has no correlation greater than 0.6 between covariates):

ggplot(div.df, aes(x = taxon_alpha.s, y = log(ins_rich))) +
     geom_point()
cor(div.df$taxon_alpha.s, log(div.df$ins_rich))
ggplot(div.df, aes(x = phylo_alpha.s, y = log(ins_rich))) +
  geom_point()

is it the clumped nature of the covariate data?

It just seems that the model is much more sensitive to design than I would expect, and it becomes difficult to do much model interpretation from the full model - which is often proposed as the best (in a Bayesian sense) approach, rather than model selection. Seems interesting to me!

Thanks again,
Colin

>
> I had a quick look at the data. Here are a few things to consider
> - the relation between taxon and phylo is strong and non-linear (log linear?)
> - the distribution of taxon is much more clumped than that of phylo
> - as a result the phylo-functional combination covers a larger part of
> the design space than the taxon-functional combination
>
> So IMHO it is not surprising that the model selects phylo + functional
> over taxon + functional
>

messages.body_plain:
I feel like we're slowly (but surely) getting there!

The issue was indeed with R version 3.5.0. I did the following tests

- R Version 3.5.0 worked perfectly with other not-inla stuff, and also with very simple inlabru models like the ones you sent us to test before the workshop (attached script)

- R Version 3.4.4 works perfectly to run the barrier model with the script you have sent me, and I manage to replicate your results.

I'll try and construct a mesh without that square and see what changes.

Virginia Morera
PhD Student
Department of Animal Biology
University of Barcelona

I am still in confusion.
As for the precision matrix, it can be get as the picture followed: (it is cut from the book "Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data")

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-gXdGqsNrYK0/WvMVmUZ3V7I/AAAAAAAAAAM/mZWHbTKYzM4kOPbsNc-y3q9apUX26kCVACLcBGAs/s1600/CAR.jpg>

As for the example you mentioned above, y_i = x_{1i} beta_{1j} + x_{2i} beta_{2j} + x_{3i} beta_{3j} + epsilon_i

We have 3 covariates and 1 observation, so we only have one value of yi. And the y in the formula is the rep(yi, 3)?

Is beta_index's function telling which covariates belong to each beta? Does Q_dependency mean the precision matrix of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3? The spatial size means the number of observation? What is the function of the parameter "group"?

A more detailed description of a my model is as follows:
I have 3 covariates x1, x2, x3. And I also have beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3. And y = x1*beta_1+x2*beta_2+x3*beta_3.
I want to estimate the value of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3 using the CAR prior. As for the prior for each beta, is a gaussian distribution where the mean is the average of that beta's neighborhood beta. And the neighborhood is determined by a known adjacent matrix.

Thank you so much for all your help.

Best Regards.

messages.body_plain:
Some more clues:

The new_sp object seems to have two components; one rectangle, and one
set of polygons that indicate what is _land_. When used as "samplers"
information, this means that lgcp will try to define the lgcp
likelihood across anywhere that isn't land, which includes part of the
mesh domain that lies outside the study domain. You'll need to
construct a samplers polygon that covers precisely the study domain;
it should be possible to get that as the difference between the
rectangle and the land polygons (that are hiding in new_sp) somehow.

You also need to supply mesh=mesh2 to the myBARRIER component definition.

Unfortunately, there is some code that then expect this to be a
regular inla.sdpe2 model object, and fails because of that. I'll keep
tracing that issue.

Finn

I constructed a polygon without the outside square to use as boundary and it does indeed change the results.

Ah, just what was needed. :-)
There will still be some issues though; even if the code might run
without mesh=mesh2, I don't think it will compute the right thing
anyway, and it fails with it there due to incorrect assumptions
elsewhere in the code.
I'll have a look after dinner...

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Re: how to add CAR prior on three fixed effect
messages.body_plain:
On 9 May 2018 at 17:18, <studywo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello,
> Thank you so much for your attention to this matter.
> I am still in confusion.
> As for the precision matrix, it can be get as the picture followed: (it is cut from the book "Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data")

That model has different variance parameters for the different components, which you didn't say anything about before.
But more crucially, it's only part of the picture. The model I described has two "dimensions"; one spatial graph index, and that graph has its own spatial adjacency structure, and one component graph index, and that adjacency describes how the components should connect to eachother instead of being independent.  So when you're talking about "the adjacency", be clear about which of the two you are referring to, and please figure out precisely what joint model for all of this it is you want. We can help with how to implement a given model, but we can't act as general statistical modelling consultants.

>
> We have 3 covariates and 1 observation, so we only have one value of yi. And the y in the formula is the rep(yi, 3)?

Very unlikely. Why would the observations be repeated?

> Is beta_index's function telling which covariates belong to each beta?

Yes.

> Does Q_dependency mean the precision matrix of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3?

See above. Q_dependency refers to the at-a-single-spatial-location dependency between the three components.

> The spatial size means the number of observation? What is the function of the parameter "group"?

I your number of observations is the same as the number of nodes in the spatial graph, yes. That is entirely up to you and how you want to define your specific model.
group indicates the indexing for the kronecker part of a kronecker precision model.

> A more detailed description of a my model is as follows:
> I have 3 covariates x1, x2, x3. And I also have beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3. And y = x1*beta_1+x2*beta_2+x3*beta_3.

Please note that this is much much less detailed than what I wrote, since you don't have any of the spatial indexes spelled out.

> I want to estimate the value of beta_1, beta_2 and beta_3 using the CAR prior. As for the prior for each beta, is a gaussian distribution where the mean is the average of that beta's neighborhood beta. And the neighborhood is determined by a known adjacent matrix.

I think you mean that their _conditional_ means are the neighbourhood averages? Otherwise you have a simultaneous autoregression model, not a CAR model (except that a SAR model can be written as a second order CAR model, but your book quote described a first order CAR model)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been trying to fit the following model in INLA:

formula_iid = inla.surv(age,status) ~ education + wealth + f(District, model="iid",graph="US.graph", values = US.gen$NAME_2, adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE)

             verbose=TRUE, control.hazard=list(model="rw1",n.intervals=20),control.inla = list(cmin = 0),
             keep=T, weights = df$weights, control.compute = list(waic=TRUE))

If I don't use "control.compute = list(waic=TRUE)", then the model runs fine and I get results. But when I use "control.compute = list(waic=TRUE)", the model runs for forever until the battery drains out and I keep seeing this on the screen:

max.logdens= -102918.7280 fn= 17 theta= 0.5547 3.7932  range=[-4.78 2.42]

file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: f83f00640846  date: Tue May 08 10:16:23 2018 +0300
Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 859, Thread: 0
Fail to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

Any idea, how to fix this?

Thanks in advance.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Predict on output of lgcp from inlabru gives unexpected result
messages.body_plain:
I've been tracing parts of the inlabru code, and there are a couple of
issues with incorrect assumptions that makes the model not do quite
the right thing, including not allowing the predict() method to do its
job properly, and handling the coordinate systems in an unforseen way
(it wants straight lines to be great circles, which deforms the
vertical line of the "bound" polygon when constructing the
likelihood).

The now too coarse domain boundary leaves some of the points outside
of the allowed domain, and it appears the code doesn't check for
that.. At first I though this is what cased the two artefacts in the
results, but that turns out not to be the case, because those effects
are still there when I remove the stray points.

Raw output plot, ignoring the Intercept:
  ggplot() + gg(mesh2, color =
exp(fit0$summary.random$myBARRIER$`0.5quant`)) + gg(bound) +
coord_equal()  ## check the rectangle is not there

This shows more of what actually happens within the study domain (with
predict(), we would be able to mask it out more easily):
  ggplot() + gg(mesh2, color = exp(pmin(0,
fit0$summary.random$myBARRIER$`0.5quant`))) + gg(bound) +
coord_equal()  ## check the rectangle is not there
It still doesn't look like a good fit to the data, but we're
definitely getting closer;
the barrier is clearly doing its job of decoupling at least point on
the mainland from the model on the ocean.  The large spatial estimated
correlation range makes it hard to see what effect the islands have;
now that we know what we're looking for in terms of boundary curves
etc, you could start increasing the detail on the bound again.

I'll look into updating the parts of the inlabru code that aren't
quite doing the right thing, but I can't make any promises regarding
when; I've already spent more time on this than I really had time for
this week.

Finn

On 9 May 2018 at 21:16, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> (it wants straight lines to be great circles, which deforms the
> vertical line of the "bound" polygon when constructing the
> likelihood).

This issue can be worked around by doing the _opposite_ of what
gSimpify does: instead of removing points that lie along straight
lines, _add_ points at regular intervals, so that you have more
control over the true shape of the polygon; a straight line in your
coordinate system is _not_ a straight line on the sphere (a great
circle) and _not_ a straight line in other projections used internally
by inlabru to construct an integration scheme in square km units.
Another possible option is to remove the crs information on all the
objects. I believe that inlabru will then simply use the raw
coordinate system, without trying to be clever.

I've attached my latest testing code.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the details, that is much clearer.
Since you don’t want dependence between the beta_k, but just within each of them, you can forget everything I wrote about a group/kronecker model, and probably go back to some of the earlier replies.

Start by constructing a model that just has _one_ beta-field. Adding the others is then just a matter of repeating the same procedure for a new column of your x-covariate matrix.

By definition, from your handwritten note, the beta models do not change over time, so this means you have a fixed player-adjacency matrix across all timepoints (since there is no time-index on beta, only player, and covariate).

Your response variable y should be the vector of all observations.
You will need an “index” vector, saying which player each observation belongs to.
Let x1 be the vector of values from the first column of the covariate matrix for all the players, ordered so that it aligns with the order of the observation vector; if element y[a] is player “i” at time “t”, then x1[a] should be x_{t,1}^i (in the notation of your note).

Define x1_effect = index
The covariate contribution in the formula is then given by
Y ~ f(x1_effect, x1, model=“besag”, ...)

Implement that first. Once you get that to work, add further terms of the same construction for x2, etc, with x2_effect=index, etc.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
Thank you so much for your prompt apply. I am sorry for that mistake.
I correct my simulation code as follows:

x11 <- rnorm(5)
x12 <- rnorm(5)
x13 <- rnorm(5)
x21 <- rnorm(5)
x22 <- rnorm(5)
x23 <- rnorm(5)
y <- 2*(x11+x21)
y <- c(y,(x12+x22))
y <- c(y,3*(x13+x23))

x1 <- c(x11,x12,x13)
x2 <- c(x21,x22,x23)

index <- rep(1:3,each=5)
adjm <- matrix(c(1,1,0,1,1,0,0,0,1),3,3)
adjm_graph <- inla.graph2matrix(adjm)
x1_effect <- index
x2_effect <- index
formula <- y ~ -1 + f(x1_effect, x1, model="besag", graph=adjm_graph)+
    f(x2_effect, x2, model="besag", graph=adjm_graph)
result <- inla(formula,family="gaussian",data=list(y=y,x1=x1,x2=x2))

Does this code look ok for you?

Thank you so much for all your help.

Best Regards.

Hi,
Reply to: Haakon, how should one interpret the Theta1 and Theta2 parameters for
the barrier model output?

The first is log(sigma) the second is log(range), so use inla.tmarginal to transform them with exponentials.

Best,
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Interpreting INLAs WAIC scores
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Interpreting INLAs WAIC scores
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colin,

The power depends on distribution of the variable. Let's assume that
we have 1000 observations of a variable X. Consider following design
options: A) 500 at -1 and 500 at +1, C) 1 at -1, 1 at +1 and 998 at 0,
C) a uniform distribution between -1 and +1. Design A has the best
power because the variance of X is the largest. Design B is worthless
because you have hardly any variance in X. Design C has less variance
than design A but can detect polynomial or non-linear relations. Since
taxon is more clumped around is mean, results in a lower variance and
hence less power.

Another thing is that the correlation between taxon and phylo is
extremely high (0.95). Those variables should never enter the model
building together, let alone be in the same model. I highly
recommended to select one of them based on ecological knowledge and
then start the model building.

Best regards,

ir. Thierry Onkelinx
Statisticus / Statistician

Vlaamse Overheid / Government of Flanders
INSTITUUT VOOR NATUUR- EN BOSONDERZOEK / RESEARCH INSTITUTE FOR NATURE
AND FOREST

thierry....@inbo.be

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

I increased gradually the complexity of the boundary (decreasing the cutoff value and the tolerance in the gsimplify function) and tested the output from the barrier model. The three images attached go from very simple boundary (cutoff = 10, the one we were using) to the more complex one (cutoff = 1). The effect seems to concentrate towards the point near the boundary were the initial model failed.

I will keep working with the normal SPDE model using this boundary (cutoff = 10) and ignoring the sampling domain as you suggested, as I still have a long way to go until I can run the definitive models... But please keep me posted of developments re using barrier models with inlabru or fixing the instabilities near the boundary.

Thank you, both, for your invaluable help!

Virginia Morera
PhD Student
Department of Animal Biology
University of Barcelona

messages.subject: Binomial under preferential sampling?
messages.subject_clean: Binomial under preferential sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Hello INLA Group!

This may be a naive question, but, is it reasonable to apply the preferential sampling approach, as described in the SPDE manual,  to a binomial (presence/absence) response?  That is, is there any reason why fitting a binomial point pattern and its associated marks jointly wouldn't be an effective strategy to deal with preferential sampling?  For example, using family = c("binomial", "binomial") or family = c("gaussian", "binomial") where both the first and second vectors consist of zeros and ones with a SPDE spatial effect on the first vector and using the "copy" feature to share the field with the second vector that also includes marks/covariates.  I've only seen examples with preferential sampling applied to a lgcp or Poisson likelihood.

Thanks,
John

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Plotting mesh using "rgl" package
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Plotting mesh using "rgl" package
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

you can use
  plot(mesh, rgl=TRUE)
to plot a mesh with rgl. See the help text for plot.inla.mesh for further options, such as the “col” and “add” arguments.

If you need more control, take a look at the plot.inla.mesh and plot.inla.trimesh code (in the mesh.R file in the code repository) to see how it uses points3d, lines3d, and triangles3d.

There is no general method that coverts inla.mesh objects to polyhedra in other formats than its own, nor as collections of polygons, partly because the sp package refuses to store polygons in 3D; they only allow 3D points in SpatialPoints objects. However, the storage format of inla.mesh is a very standard triangulation graph representation;
Points: mesh$loc, one point per row
Triangle-vertex index matrix: mesh$graph$tv, in counterclockwise order for each triangle.
The mesh$graph collection also has a few more elements for convenience.

Finn

Sure, you can use one data set to fit the model and then predict it to another dataset. However. INLA does the model fitting and prediction in one go. So you need to combine the training data and the test data into one data set. And set the response variable of the test part to NA. Then the test data is not used to fit the model.

with this, you can have a linear predictor model for both p, and the

there is a discussion of this issue (about rain-fall) in the spde-
tutorial.

H

messages.body_plain:
So I am trying to apply a method of hurdle model i found in marta blangiardo and Michela camelettis book but i am not sure how to go about finishing this code. I feel the problem comes from manipulating the stack.

Any help?

pred.cords <- cbind(df$Longitude, df$Latitude)
boundary <- inla.nonconvex.hull(points = pred.cords,
                                convex = 0.2, concave = 0.2)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = pred.cords, boundary = boundary,
                     max.edge = c(0.3,1.2), cutoff = 0.1)

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = pred.cords)
dim(A)

plot(mesh)

z <- as.numeric(df$pledgedUSD > 0)

y <- ifelse(df$pledgedUSD > 0, df$pledgedUSD, NA)

stk.y <- inla.stack(data = list(amount = y,
                                alldata = cbind(y, NA)),
                    A = list(A,1),
                    effects = list(
                      list(y.field = 1:spde$n.spde),
                      list(y.intercept = rep(1,length(y))),
                      list(c(df$goal,df$Categories,df$City_Pop,df$Length_of_kick,df$Days_spent_making_campign,
                             df$Twords))),
                    tag = "est.y")

stk.z <- inla.stack(data = list(occurence = z,
                                alldata = cbind(NA, z)),
                    A = list(A,1),
                    effects = list(
                      list(z.field = 1:spde$n.spde),
                      list(z.intercept = rep(1,length(z))),
                      list(c(df$goal,df$Categories,df$City_Pop,df$Length_of_kick,df$Days_spent_making_campign,
                             df$Twords))),
                    tag = "est.z")

stk.yz <- inla.stack(stk.y,stk.z)

formula.yz <- alldata ~ y.intercept + z.intercept + goal + Twords + City_Pop + Length_of_kick +
  Days_spent_making_campign  + Categories +
  f(y.field, model = spde) + f(z.field, model = spde) +
  f(year, model = "rw2") +
  f(zc.field, copy = "y.field", fixed = FALSE)

out.yz <-inla(
  formula.yz, family = c("poisson","binomial"),
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.yz),
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.yz)),
  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, config = TRUE),
  control.inla = list(strategy = "laplace")
)

messages.body_plain:
I have a dataset of hourly traffic counts at 96 signalised intersections. The data is recorded over six months. I am obtaining reasonable predictions for the final day after running the model for eight weeks prior. However this is specifying an iid interaction between space and time. I would like to try the interaction between structured space and structured time, but the model is crashing. Is this the correct way to specify the model?
ID.area.int <- data.subset$ID #Intersections 1 to 96
ID.year.int <http://id.year.int/> <- data.subset$Time #Time 1 to 1344 per ID
formula.intIV = Y ~ f(ID, model = "bym", graph = H) + f(Time,model="seasonal",season.length=48) + f(Time1, model = "iid") + f(ID.area.int <http://id.area.int/>, model="besag", graph = H, group = ID.year.int <http://id.year.int/>, control.group = list(model = "rw2"))
mod.intIV <- inla(formula.intIV,family="poisson",data = data.subset, control.predictor=list(link = 1, compute = TRUE), verbose = T)
I have tried changing the number of threads and 'control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"))'. It is running for several hours, then crashes with a Windows dialog 'inla.exe has crashed'. Am I specifying the interaction correctly?

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am reading the section 8.2 in the Blangiardo and Cameletti book (page 270), and I wonder if there is an errata in page 279. They check the significance of the spatial effects by running the complete range of possible models; in particular, in the model including only the spatial component shared by both responses, they use the following syntax for the formula:

form.oneshared <- alldata ~ -1 + y.intercept + z.intercept + f(y.field, model=spde) + f(z.field, model=spde)

where y.field is the spatial random effect for the gamma distributed response and z.field is the spatial random effect  for the Bernoulli distributed response (page 275).

I wonder if the code should be as follows:

formula.yz <- alldata ~ -1 + y.intercept + z.intercept + f(y.field, model=spde) + f(zc.field, copy="y.field", fixed=FALSE)

I would like to know if I am wrong in order to be sure that I correctly understood the syntax.

Thank you in advance.

Juan Miguel

messages.body_plain:
I have tried beta, but INLA does not accept 0-s and 1-s as beta-distributed data, which actually seems sensible to me. The beta-density is either 0 or INF at an end point. In my case the density is necessarily INF because of overdispersion.

The binomial nature of the beta-binomial is precisely why it works for both 0-s and 1-s. I have been wrong in accepting in-between values in this case, though. The betabinomial seems well defined as a continuous density for continuous N > 1. See: http://ac.inf.elte.hu/Vol_039_2013/137_39.pdf. Hence, Ntrials need to be larger than 1. But what does actually INLA do with non-integer values of Ntrials and x? Follow the paper largely, or something else?

best
Øyvind

messages.subject: Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object
messages.subject_clean: Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to reconcile the notation used in Lindgren et al. 2011 with the elements of an `inla.spde2` object.
Ultimately, I'd like to use Eq 22 in Appendix 3 of LIndgren et al. 2011 to implement a nonstationary model
in a separate software package (Template Model Builder), using covariates for κ and τ. Fixing α = 2,
Equation 22 gives:

Q = τ(κ²Cκ² + κ²G + Gκ² + GC⁻¹G)τ

where κ and τ are diagonal matrices taking the values of κ(sᵢ) and τ(sᵢ) at the mesh node locations. Looking
at the implementation used to find the precision matrix in the R source for the `inla.spde2.precision`, I see

    Q = (D0 %*% (D1 %*% spde$param.inla$M0 %*% D1 +
                 D12 %*% spde$param.inla$M1 +
                 t(spde$param.inla$M1) %*% D12 +
                 spde$param.inla$M2) %*% D0)

It appears then that the different elements are:
`D0` is τ, with elements determined by the regression
`D1` is κ², also based on a regression specification
`D12` is κ² times another diagonal matrix that is determined by the link function?
`M0` is C
`M1` is G
`M2` is GC⁻¹G
I then have two questions:
Are these all correct?
When is `D12` different from `D1`?
Conceptually, why is `D1`/κ² different in the term with `M0` versus `D12` in the term with `M1`?
Sorry if these are covered elsewhere. I've been working on understanding the SPDE approximation for a
while, but it's starting to come together (thanks in part to Haakon Bakka's explainer on the arXiv, which I
found very helpful).

Thank you,

John Best

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

to implement your own SPDE models, I would strongly recommend _not_
extracting the matrices from an inla.spde object, since those are tied
to the internal representation of a family of models including alpha
between 0 and 2, oscillating models, and nonstationary models, all as
described in the Lindgren,Rue,Lindström 2011 JRSSB paper.  Instead I
would recommend using inla.mesh.fem() to obtain the C, G, G2=GC^-1G
building block matrices directly and build your code around that.  You
can of course still use the inla.spde2.matern and inla.spde2.generic
code to draw inspiration from!

That said, your interpretation of what you found in the object/code is correct.
D12 is different from D1 for oscillating (non-Matérn) models; the
basic oscillating model can be parameterised like this
  tau^2 (kappa^4 C + 2 kappa^2 gamma G + GC^-1G),
where gamma is > -1.

I've attached the original design document for the inla.spde2 model family.

Finn

> `M0` is C
> `M1` is G
> `M2` is GC⁻¹G
>

>
> Are these all correct?
> When is `D12` different from `D1`?
> Conceptually, why is `D1`/κ² different in the term with `M0` versus `D12` in

>

> SPDE approximation for a
> while, but it's starting to come together (thanks in part to Haakon Bakka's
> explainer on the arXiv, which I
> found very helpful).
>
> Thank you,

messages.subject: RStudio + INLA using Docker
messages.subject_clean: RStudio + INLA using Docker
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I managed to create a Docker image containing RStudio + INLA package.
The RStudio is the server version, so it is used through a web browser (Similar interface compared to the standalone version).
I did this to avoid frequent issues as:
Different environments causes results mismatch.
Difficulties reproducing results.
Trying out a new version.
I believe having RStudio with INLA in a docker container helps solving those issues.

The docker images are hosted in Docker Hub, and there are two version:
Stable version <https://hub.docker.com/r/egonzalf/inla-stable-rstudio/>
Testing version <https://hub.docker.com/r/egonzalf/inla-testing-rstudio/>
built from the respective repository.

I also prepared a bash script (for Linux/Unix/MacOS) to help launching the RStudio server. It can be found in GitHub <https://github.com/egonzalf/rstudio-inla>
git clone https://github.com/egonzalf/rstudio-inla.git
cd rstudio-inla
./run-rstudio.sh

You can run ./run-rstudio.sh --help for more options.

To get started with docker and how to install it, please visit:
https://www.docker.com/community-edition

Hope this will be useful to somebody.
Best regards,

Ah, I missed that, sorry.
Those theta results perfectly match your true parameters; theta1=log(3) is just above 1, as is the posterior mean; and 0 is also in the credible interval for theta2.
To see that in the natural scale (range and variance), please use inla.spde.result()

2018-05-29 14:25 GMT+02:00 Eduardo Gonzalez Fisher <eduardo.gon...@gmail.com>:

> Hi everyone,
>
> I managed to create a Docker image containing RStudio + INLA package.
> The RStudio is the server version, so it is used through a web browser (Similar interface compared to the standalone version).
> I did this to avoid frequent issues as:
> Different environments causes results mismatch.
> Difficulties reproducing results.
> Trying out a new version.
> I believe having RStudio with INLA in a docker container helps solving those issues.
>
> The docker images are hosted in Docker Hub, and there are two version:
> Stable version <https://hub.docker.com/r/egonzalf/inla-stable-rstudio/>
> Testing version <https://hub.docker.com/r/egonzalf/inla-testing-rstudio/>
> built from the respective repository.
>
> I also prepared a bash script (for Linux/Unix/MacOS) to help launching the RStudio server. It can be found in GitHub <https://github.com/egonzalf/rstudio-inla>
> git clone https://github.com/egonzalf/rstudio-inla.git
> cd rstudio-inla
> ./run-rstudio.sh
>
> You can run ./run-rstudio.sh --help for more options.
>
> To get started with docker and how to install it, please visit:
> https://www.docker.com/community-edition
>
>

messages.subject: a question of separable space-time model
messages.subject_clean: a question of separable space-time model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA developers

It is clear that INLA can deal with space time model with separable variance covariance matrix.
E.g. In Cameletti's case, they use an additive form to capture the real spatiotemporal effects.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Tav5VYC_icc/Ww2EPDx3hdI/AAAAAAAAETU/jNlFp5Yz4xgeG6vZQyWao1Sk7tml_y5_ACLcBGAs/s1600/1.gif>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Sn6AnWInF7I/Ww2EWH2HvHI/AAAAAAAAETY/xUbnNid5B1g2R7v_yjm3lD7L_rpRZpt4wCLcBGAs/s1600/2.gif>

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-vIh-9V0WBXc/Ww2EYuTpFNI/AAAAAAAAETc/d5R2Sxs6rkUK5qkIYdyOpEKFSEN5ODMoQCLcBGAs/s1600/4.gif>

Indeed, I would like to know if INLA can deal with the following model, with a product formed variance covariance matrix?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Y2i4zfGMcII/Ww2GeZ7ZmaI/AAAAAAAAETw/eFSrYsGoj6I8T_TQMkuZR1nvYS5cMRUXQCLcBGAs/s1600/CodeCogsEqn.gif>

Example cases exist?

Thanks
LING

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] a question of separable space-time model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] a question of separable space-time model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
In the Cameletti et al case, the covariance of \xi also takes a product form; it's the product of a Matern covariance in space and an exponential covariance in time.
That model was specified using an "ar1" "group" model, which defines a kronecker product precision matrix model, which exactly translates into a product of covariance functions.
See ?control.group for a list of other supported models to use in that kind of construction.
For more general models, you can define your own using the rgeneric model framework (search the list for previous mentions of rgeneric models)

Finn
